questions.stem: A 60-year-old man with new AKI is being evaluated. Which is the most appropriate FIRST imaging study?
explanations: Incorrect. Avoid contrast in AKI when possible.

Correct. RENAL ULTRASOUND is the FIRST-LINE imaging in AKI. Provides: kidney size and echogenicity, presence of HYDRONEPHROSIS (post-renal obstruction — must rule out promptly), masses, cysts, vascular Doppler. Bedside, no contrast, no radiation. Limitations: operator-dependent; less sensitive for stones than CT; difficult in obese patients. Other indications: CKD evaluation, hematuria, transplant kidney monitoring, renal artery stenosis screening (Doppler).
Incorrect. MRI is more for masses, vascular complex.

questions.stem: A 50-year-old man with severe flank pain and hematuria has imaging concerning for kidney stone. Which is the MOST sensitive imaging study for renal stones?
explanations: Correct. NON-CONTRAST CT (low-dose 'CT KUB' or stone protocol CT) is the GOLD STANDARD for kidney stone diagnosis: sensitivity ~95%, specificity ~95%. Detects radio-opaque AND radiolucent stones (uric acid, cystine), measures size precisely, shows ureteral location, hydronephrosis, alternative diagnoses. Disadvantages: ionizing radiation (low-dose protocols reduce this). ULTRASOUND is alternative for: pregnancy (avoid radiation), pediatrics, repeated imaging follow-up; sensitivity ~85% but lower for ureteral stones. KUB has limited role.
Incorrect. US is less sensitive but used in pregnancy.
Incorrect. MRI is not ideal for stones (Ca doesn't show well on MRI).

questions.stem: A 65-year-old man with worsening hypertension and difficult-to-control BP is suspected of having renal artery stenosis. Which is the most appropriate initial imaging modality?
explanations: Correct. RENAL ARTERY STENOSIS imaging hierarchy: (1) DOPPLER ULTRASOUND — useful screening (peak systolic velocity, resistive index), operator-dependent; (2) CT ANGIOGRAPHY (CTA) — high sensitivity/specificity, but contrast load; (3) MAGNETIC RESONANCE ANGIOGRAPHY (MRA) — comparable accuracy without iodinated contrast (gadolinium concerns in CKD though limited with newer agents); (4) RENAL ANGIOGRAM — gold standard, allows intervention (angioplasty/stent), but invasive. Captopril renogram is functional test but largely supplanted by CTA/MRA. Decision based on patient factors (CKD, contrast allergy, suspicion).
Incorrect. DMSA is for cortical scarring.

questions.stem: A 50-year-old woman with hematuria and concern for urothelial malignancy is being evaluated. Which best characterizes the recommended imaging?
explanations: Correct. Hematuria evaluation in adults (especially with risk factors — age >35, smoking, occupational exposures): CT UROGRAM (CTU) — multiphase contrast CT with non-contrast, nephrographic, and excretory phases; evaluates kidneys, ureters, bladder for stones, masses, urothelial cancer. Plus CYSTOSCOPY for direct bladder evaluation (urothelial cancer most often in bladder; ~5% in upper tract). MR urography is alternative if contrast contraindicated. AUA guidelines stratify by risk; not all microhematuria requires full workup. Painless gross hematuria + smoking history → bladder cancer until proven otherwise.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old man with CKD stage 4 needs imaging for suspected renal mass. Which best characterizes contrast considerations?
choices: Iodinated contrast is safe in CKD 4
Risk of contrast nephropathy and NSF
No imaging is possible in CKD
explanations: Correct. Imaging in advanced CKD: IODINATED CONTRAST — risk of contrast-induced nephropathy / contrast-associated AKI (CIN/CA-AKI) — especially eGFR <30. Mitigation: hydration, lowest volume, alternative imaging. GADOLINIUM (for MRI) — historical concern for NEPHROGENIC SYSTEMIC FIBROSIS (NSF) in advanced CKD/dialysis, particularly with older Gd agents (gadolinium chloride, gadodiamide). Newer macrocyclic Gd agents are considered safer. Modern guidelines often allow contrast use with appropriate risk-benefit consideration. ALTERNATIVE: non-contrast CT, ultrasound, MRI without contrast, or carefully justified contrast study with informed consent.
Incorrect. Specific risk in advanced CKD.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old woman with new bilateral renal cysts on ultrasound has a family history of similar disease. Genetic testing for ADPKD is positive. Which best characterizes the imaging features of ADPKD?
explanations: Correct. Autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease imaging: MULTIPLE BILATERAL RENAL CYSTS of varying sizes (often hundreds), enlarging both kidneys progressively. Liver cysts in 80% (often coexisting). Diagnosis criteria (Ravine): age 15–39 with 3+ cysts uni- or bilaterally; 40–59 with 2+ in each kidney; >60 with 4+ in each. Cerebral aneurysms in ~10% (screen with MRA in family history of subarachnoid hemorrhage). Other extra-renal: mitral valve prolapse, colonic diverticula. Tolvaptan slows progression. Ultrasound is first-line; MRI for total kidney volume estimation (predicts progression).
Incorrect. Glomerular not seen on imaging.

questions.stem: A 4-year-old child with recurrent UTI is being evaluated for vesicoureteral reflux (VUR). Which is the appropriate imaging?
explanations: Incorrect. MRI is not principal for VUR.

Correct. VOIDING CYSTOURETHROGRAM (VCUG) — fluoroscopic study filling the bladder with contrast and observing during voiding to detect vesicoureteral reflux (VUR — urine refluxing back up the ureters into the kidneys). Indications: recurrent febrile UTI in children, abnormal renal ultrasound findings (hydronephrosis), antenatal hydronephrosis. Grades I-V (severity). Higher grades increase risk of pyelonephritis and renal scarring. Treatment: prophylactic antibiotics, surgical reimplantation (Cohen, Lich-Gregoir) for high-grade VUR. Radioisotope cystogram is an alternative with less radiation.
Incorrect. Cystoscopy is bladder-only, not for reflux assessment.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old man with recurrent pyelonephritis has imaging to assess for renal scarring. Which best characterizes the imaging modality?
explanations: Correct. DMSA (DIMERCAPTOSUCCINIC ACID) — radioisotope renal scan; concentrates in proximal tubular cells, providing CORTICAL imaging. Indications: detection of CORTICAL SCARRING (chronic pyelonephritis, congenital scars), assessment of split renal function (each kidney's contribution to total). Acute pyelonephritis shows photopenic defects. Cleared from circulation slowly (vs MAG3 for tubular function/perfusion). DTPA is for filtration / GFR measurement. MAG3 (mercaptoacetyltriglycine) — combined glomerular and tubular function assessment.
Incorrect. Plain X-ray is not for scarring.

questions.stem: A 50-year-old man with possible renal artery stenosis is undergoing captopril renogram. Which best characterizes the test?
explanations: Correct. CAPTOPRIL RENOGRAM — renal scintigraphy (typically MAG3 or DTPA) before and after ACE inhibitor administration. In RAS, the ACE inhibitor blocks angiotensin II-mediated efferent constriction that normally maintains GFR distal to the stenosis; the affected kidney's perfusion/function falls dramatically post-captopril, while the contralateral side is preserved. This relative change supports RAS. Largely SUPPLANTED by CTA/MRA in modern practice (anatomic imaging more direct). Still useful in selected cases.

questions.stem: A 50-year-old man has incidentally discovered renal mass on CT. Which best characterizes the imaging assessment of solid renal masses?
explanations: Incorrect. Many solid masses are RCC or other malignancy.

Correct. Solid renal mass evaluation: CT or MRI WITH CONTRAST (multiphase: non-contrast, corticomedullary, nephrographic, excretory) to characterize. ENHANCEMENT >15–20 HU on CT after contrast → solid component → likely neoplasm. RCC features: heterogeneous enhancement, hemorrhage, necrosis, occasional calcification, vascular invasion (renal vein, IVC). ANGIOMYOLIPOMA (benign) — fat density (negative HU) is diagnostic. ONCOCYTOMA — benign but often indistinguishable from RCC on imaging; biopsy or surgery for confirmation. Bosniak classification for cystic masses (I–IV) guides management.

questions.stem: A 35-year-old man with severe flank pain has imaging showing hyperdense mass at the renal pelvis with hydronephrosis. Which best characterizes the differential?
explanations: Correct. Hyperdense mass at the renal pelvis with hydronephrosis — STONE most common (high HU, often >300, calcified). Other considerations: urothelial mass (transitional cell carcinoma — heterogeneous enhancement); blood clot (recent trauma or anticoagulation); fungal ball (immunocompromised, especially Candida); sloughed papilla (papillary necrosis from analgesics, sickle cell, NSAIDs). CT urogram with delayed phase (excretory) helps characterize. Biopsy or surgical exploration may be needed for definitive diagnosis if not obviously a stone.
Incorrect. Glomerular not seen on imaging.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old man with painless gross hematuria and smoking history has CT urogram showing a filling defect in the bladder. Which best characterizes the next step?
explanations: Correct. Painless gross hematuria + smoking + filling defect on imaging → BLADDER CANCER until proven otherwise. CYSTOSCOPY WITH BIOPSY is the diagnostic gold standard for bladder cancer, allows visualization, biopsy, and staging. Transurethral resection (TURBT) provides histologic diagnosis and initial treatment for non-muscle-invasive cancer. Risk factors for urothelial cancer: SMOKING (most important; 50% of bladder cancers), occupational exposures (aromatic amines — rubber, dye, leather, petrochemical), schistosomiasis (squamous cell), cyclophosphamide, radiation. CT urogram + cystoscopy together cover upper and lower urinary tract.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old researcher considers Bosniak classification of renal cysts. Which best characterizes the system?
explanations: Correct. BOSNIAK classification of renal cysts (radiologic): I — simple (water density, smooth thin wall, no enhancement) — BENIGN, no follow-up needed. II — minimally complex (thin septations, fine calcifications), benign, no follow-up. IIF — moderately complex (more septations, higher density), follow-up imaging. III — indeterminate (thicker walls or septations, irregular calcifications, possible enhancement), 50–60% malignancy risk → SURGERY usually. IV — frankly malignant features (enhancing soft tissue, mural nodules) → high malignancy risk → surgery. Newer Bosniak 2019 incorporates MRI features. Important for management decisions.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old researcher considers renal angiography indications. Which best characterizes the role of formal renal angiogram in modern practice?
choices: Reserved for therapy or unclear diagnosis
explanations: Correct. RENAL ANGIOGRAPHY — invasive procedure with iodinated contrast and arterial access. Modern indications: (1) THERAPEUTIC — angioplasty / stenting of renal artery stenosis, embolization (renal mass, AVM, post-trauma bleeding), tumor embolization before nephrectomy, kidney biopsy of vascular lesions; (2) DIAGNOSTIC — selected cases where less invasive imaging (CTA, MRA) is inconclusive; vasculitis assessment (microaneurysms in PAN). Risks: contrast nephropathy, atheroembolism (cholesterol crystal embolization → AKI, livedo reticularis, eosinophilia, low complement), bleeding, dissection. Largely supplanted by CTA/MRA for diagnostic purposes.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old researcher considers imaging in pregnancy. Which best characterizes the recommended approach in suspected nephrolithiasis in pregnancy?
explanations: Correct. Imaging in pregnancy: AVOID IONIZING RADIATION when possible, especially in 1st trimester. ULTRASOUND first-line for: nephrolithiasis (less sensitive than CT but no radiation), AKI, hydronephrosis, masses. Limitations: less sensitive than CT for ureteral stones; physiologic hydronephrosis of pregnancy (right > left from gravid uterus compression) can mimic obstruction. MR UROGRAPHY (without gadolinium ideally) is alternative in 2nd/3rd trimester for unclear cases. LOW-DOSE NON-CONTRAST CT only when clinically essential. Gadolinium concerns in pregnancy (older agents); modern macrocyclic Gd if needed in compelling cases.
Incorrect. MRI may be needed but US first.

questions.stem: A 50-year-old patient with chronic loin pain has imaging showing 'ring sign' on contrast study suggesting papillary necrosis. Which condition best fits?
explanations: Correct. PAPILLARY NECROSIS — ischemic injury to renal medullary papillae. Causes (mnemonic POSTCARDS): Pyelonephritis, Obstruction, Sickle cell disease, TB, Cirrhosis, Analgesic abuse, Renal vein thrombosis, Diabetes, Systemic vasculitis. Imaging: 'RING SIGN' on excretory phase (contrast around the necrotic papilla); cavities, sloughed papillae causing distal obstruction. Hematuria, sterile pyuria, recurrent UTI, AKI from ureteral obstruction by sloughed tissue. Treatment: address underlying cause; relieve obstruction.
Incorrect. Glomerular not seen on imaging.

questions.stem: A 75-year-old man has bilateral renal artery stenosis confirmed on CTA. Which best characterizes the imaging finding for diagnostic significance?
explanations: Incorrect. Insufficient narrowing for clinical relevance.

Correct. HEMODYNAMICALLY SIGNIFICANT renal artery stenosis: >70–75% LUMEN NARROWING; or peak systolic velocity >180–200 cm/s on Doppler ultrasound; or translesional pressure gradient >10–20 mm Hg at angiogram. Causes: ATHEROSCLEROSIS (most common, elderly, ostial/proximal); FIBROMUSCULAR DYSPLASIA (younger women, mid/distal vessel, 'string of beads' appearance). Manifestations: refractory HTN (often new onset or sudden worsening), AKI on ACE inhibitor, asymmetric kidney size, audible bruit. Treatment: medical optimization first; angioplasty/stent for selected (CORAL trial — modest benefit, not for all).

questions.stem: A 30-year-old researcher reviews ultrasound findings in CKD. Which best characterizes the typical sonographic features?
explanations: Correct. CKD ultrasound features: SMALL KIDNEYS (<9 cm in adult), INCREASED CORTICAL ECHOGENICITY (cortex brighter than liver/spleen — reflects fibrosis/scarring), CORTICAL THINNING, loss of corticomedullary differentiation. Kidney size >9 cm with normal echogenicity in CKD suggests potentially reversible cause or recent onset. Conditions where CKD has LARGE kidneys: diabetic nephropathy (early), HIV-associated nephropathy, amyloidosis, polycystic kidney disease, infiltrative disease (myeloma, lymphoma). Imaging guides diagnosis and biopsy decisions; small kidneys generally do not warrant biopsy (low yield, high bleeding risk).

questions.stem: A 60-year-old woman with new AKI has ultrasound showing bilateral hydronephrosis. Which best characterizes the workup?
explanations: Correct. Bilateral hydronephrosis suggests bladder outlet or BILATERAL ureteral obstruction. Workup: (1) Bladder catheterization first (relieves bladder outlet obstruction immediately if BPH); (2) CT abdomen/pelvis (often without contrast initially in AKI) to identify cause: BPH, bladder cancer, prostate cancer, malignant ureteral obstruction (gynecologic, GI, lymph nodes, metastatic), retroperitoneal fibrosis, stones; (3) Urology consultation for definitive treatment: prostate management, ureteral stents, percutaneous nephrostomy, surgical debulking. Post-obstructive diuresis monitoring after relief. AKI typically reverses with timely intervention.
Incorrect. No biopsy needed for obstruction.
Incorrect. Diet is not the principal step.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old researcher considers renal biopsy imaging guidance. Which best characterizes the modality?
explanations: Correct. Renal biopsy GUIDANCE: ULTRASOUND-GUIDED PERCUTANEOUS biopsy is the standard approach (lower pole of kidney to avoid hilar vessels). CT-GUIDED for difficult cases (obese patients, deep kidneys, transplant biopsies in difficult location). LAPAROSCOPIC OR OPEN biopsy reserved for cases when percutaneous fails. Native kidney biopsy: post-procedure monitoring 4–6 hours (or overnight) for bleeding. Transplant biopsy: similar approach. Major risks: bleeding (10% gross hematuria, 1% transfusion, rare surgery for pole avulsion or AVF formation), pain, infection.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old researcher considers DTPA renogram. Which best characterizes the test?
explanations: Correct. DTPA (diethylenetriaminepentaacetic acid) renogram — IV-administered radioisotope, freely filtered (like inulin), no tubular reabsorption or secretion. Used to: (1) MEASURE GFR (single kidney or combined); (2) RENOGRAM CURVE — perfusion phase, filtration phase, excretion phase; assesses obstruction (delayed excretion); RAS (delayed perfusion); transplant kidney function. MAG3 (mercaptoacetyltriglycine) — alternative, also tubular function (better in low-GFR or pediatric patients). DMSA — cortical imaging (scarring). Renal scintigraphy is FUNCTIONAL imaging complementing anatomic CT/US.

questions.stem: A 50-year-old man with acute right flank pain and microscopic hematuria has CT showing 5 mm stone in mid-ureter with mild proximal hydronephrosis. Which best characterizes the management implication?
explanations: Correct. Ureteral stone passage rates depend on size and location: <5 mm → ~80% pass spontaneously; 5–7 mm → ~50%; >7 mm → unlikely to pass. Distal ureter passes more easily than proximal. Conservative management: hydration, analgesia (NSAIDs preferred over opioids if no AKI), MEDICAL EXPULSIVE THERAPY (tamsulosin α-blocker — modest evidence; debated). Indications for surgical/endoscopic intervention: failed expulsive therapy, large stone, infection (urgent decompression), refractory pain, AKI. Options: ESWL (extracorporeal shock-wave lithotripsy), URETEROSCOPY with laser lithotripsy, percutaneous nephrolithotomy (large stones).

questions.stem: A 45-year-old woman with renal mass on imaging has features suggesting fat density (negative Hounsfield units). Which best characterizes this imaging finding?
explanations: Incorrect. RCC does not have fat density.

Correct. ANGIOMYOLIPOMA (AML) — benign tumor composed of vascular, smooth muscle, and FAT components. CT shows characteristic FAT DENSITY (negative HU, <-20). Diagnostic by imaging alone (no biopsy needed in classic appearance). Solitary AMLs are usually sporadic; multiple bilateral AMLs suggest TUBEROUS SCLEROSIS COMPLEX (genetic, AML + cardiac rhabdomyoma + cortical tubers + ash-leaf macules + facial angiofibromas). Management: small (<4 cm) — observation; larger or symptomatic — selective embolization or partial nephrectomy (rupture risk with tumors >4 cm). Aggressive resection avoided to preserve nephrons. mTOR inhibitors (sirolimus, everolimus) shrink AMLs in TSC.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old researcher considers retroperitoneal fibrosis imaging. Which best characterizes the findings?
explanations: Incorrect. Not principally a kidney mass.

Correct. RETROPERITONEAL FIBROSIS — mantle of fibrotic tissue surrounding aorta, IVC, and ureters in retroperitoneum. Imaging (CT or MRI): SOFT-TISSUE MANTLE around aorta extending to encase ureters; URETERS MEDIALLY DEVIATED (vs lateral with retroperitoneal masses); BILATERAL HYDRONEPHROSIS from ureteral obstruction. Causes: idiopathic (Ormond disease, often IgG4-related), drugs (methysergide, ergot alkaloids, β-blockers, methyldopa, hydralazine), aortic aneurysm, malignancy, radiation, infection. Treatment: corticosteroids (idiopathic), tamoxifen, ureteral stents/nephrostomy for obstruction, surgical ureterolysis. PET-CT to assess malignancy.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old researcher considers renal transplant imaging. Which best characterizes ultrasound monitoring of a transplant kidney?
explanations: Correct. Transplant kidney imaging — routine monitoring, especially in early postoperative period: KIDNEY SIZE; HYDRONEPHROSIS (ureteral kink/stenosis, BPH; lymphocele compressing); PERINEPHRIC COLLECTIONS — hematoma (early, often resolves), lymphocele (peri-lymphatic disruption, late, often asymptomatic; symptomatic ones need drainage), urinoma (anastomotic leak), abscess; VASCULAR DOPPLER — renal artery patency, resistive index (RI elevated in rejection or thrombosis), arterial stenosis (anastomotic, post-transplant). Biopsy guides definitive diagnosis when ultrasound suggests rejection or other intrinsic dysfunction.
